Questions: Why is the current provided by a cell called a direct current (d.c.)?
Answers: only flows in one direction

Questions: What is an alternating current (a.c.)?
Answers: current that repeatedly reverses direction

Questions: What kind of current is supplied by mains electricity?
Answers: alternating current

Questions: What is the frequency and voltage of mains electricity?
What colours are the live, neutral, and earth wires in a three-core cable?
Answers: live = brown, neutral = blue, earth = green and yellow stripes

Questions: What is the function of the live wire in a three-core cable?
Answers: carries the alternating potential difference from the supply

Questions: What is the function of the neutral wire in a three-core cable?
Answers: Completes the circuit and carries current back to the supply.

Questions: What is the function of the earth wire in a three-core cable?
Answers: Carries fault current to earth, causing the fuse or circuit breaker to disconnect the supply.

Questions: When is there a current in the earth wire?
Answers: If a fault connects the live wire to the earthed case.

Questions: Why is the live wire dangerous?
Answers: Touching it can drive current through a person to earth, causing electric shock.

Questions: What is the National Grid?
Answers: nationwide network of cables and transformers that link power stations to customers

Questions: What are step-up transformers used for in the National Grid?
Answers: increase the p.d. from the power station to the transmission cables

Questions: What are step-down transformers used for in the National Grid?
Answers: Reduce the transmission p.d. to the 230 V mains supply.

Questions: Why does the National Grid use a high transmission voltage?
Answers: At the same power, higher p.d. means lower current and less heating loss in the cables.

Questions: What two things does energy transfer to an appliance depend on?
Answers: power of appliance; time it is switched on for

Questions: What are the units for power, current, potential difference, and resistance?
Answers: watts (W), amps (A), volts (V), ohms (Ω)

Questions: Which two quantities do you need to measure to find the density of a solid or liquid?
Answers: mass and volume

Questions: What happens to the particles in a substance if its temperature is increased?
Answers: Their average kinetic energy increases, so they move faster.

Questions: Why are changes of state physical changes?
Answers: No new substance forms; reversing the change restores the original material.

Questions: Why is the mass of a substance conserved when it changes state?
Answers: the number of particles does not change

Questions: What is the internal energy of a substance?
Answers: the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in the substance

Questions: Why does temperature stay constant during a change of state?
Answers: Energy changes the particles’ potential energy, not their average kinetic energy.

Questions: What is the name given to the energy transferred when a substance changes state?
Answers: latent heat

Questions: What is the specific latent heat of a substance?
Answers: the energy required to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change

Questions: What is the specific latent heat of fusion of a substance?
Answers: the energy to change 1 kg from solid to liquid at its melting point, with no temperature change

Questions: What is the specific latent heat of vaporisation of a substance?
Answers: the energy to change 1 kg from liquid to vapour at its boiling point, with no temperature change

Questions: On a temperature–time graph, what do the flat (horizontal) sections show?
Answers: times when the substance is changing state and temperature is not changing

Questions: What property of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its particles?
Answers: Temperature: higher temperature means higher average kinetic energy.

Questions: What causes the pressure of a gas on a surface?
Answers: the force of gas particles hitting the surface

Questions: Give two reasons why the pressure of a gas in a sealed container increases if its temperature is increased.
Answers: Particles hit the walls more often and transfer more momentum in each collision.

Questions: Give two reasons why the temperature of a gas increases if it is compressed quickly.
Answers: Work done on the gas increases its internal energy; little energy escapes during rapid compression.

Questions: Why does increasing a gas’s volume lower its pressure at constant temperature?
Answers: Particles travel further between wall collisions, so there are fewer collisions each second.

Questions: Name five common energy stores.
Answers: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical

Questions: Name four ways energy can be transferred.
Answers: by heating, by waves, by electric current, by forces doing work

Questions: What is a system?
Answers: an object or group of objects

Questions: What is a closed system?
Answers: A system with no energy transfer to or from its surroundings.

Questions: What is work done?
Answers: Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance.

Questions: What is the unit for energy?
Answers: joules (J)

Questions: What is one joule of work?
Answers: the work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force

Questions: Describe the energy transfer when a moving car slows down.
Answers: Energy moves from the car’s kinetic store to the thermal stores of the brakes and surroundings.

Questions: Describe the energy transfer when an electric kettle is used to heat water.
Answers: Electric current heats the element; energy then transfers by heating to the water.

Questions: Describe the energy transfer when a ball is fired using an elastic band.
Answers: Energy transfers from the band’s elastic potential store to the ball’s kinetic store.

Questions: Describe the energy transfer when a battery‑powered toy car is used.
Answers: Chemical energy in the battery transfers electrically to the car’s kinetic store; some warms the surroundings.

Questions: Describe the energy transfer when a falling apple hits the ground.
Answers: Apple kinetic store to thermal stores of the apple and ground; some energy leaves as sound.

Questions: Name the unit that represents one joule transferred per second.
Answers: watt (W)

Questions: A motor is 30% efficient. What does that mean?
Answers: 30% of energy is usefully transferred; 70% is dissipated

Questions: What is stopping distance?
Answers: Thinking distance plus braking distance.

Questions: What is thinking distance?
Answers: Distance travelled during the driver’s reaction time.

Questions: What is braking distance?
Answers: Distance travelled after the brakes are applied.

Questions: What is the relationship between stopping distance, thinking distance, and braking distance?
Answers: stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

Questions: Does the speed of a vehicle have a bigger effect on braking distance or thinking distance?
Answers: braking distance

Questions: At fixed reaction time, which stopping-distance component is proportional to speed?
Answers: Thinking distance.

Questions: What are three factors that can affect the braking distance of a vehicle?
Answers: speed, road conditions, condition of tyres and brakes

Questions: What can happen if the braking force used to stop a vehicle is very large?
Answers: The brakes may overheat or the wheels may skid.

Questions: What is the law of conservation of momentum?
Answers: in a closed system, total momentum before an event equals total momentum after

Questions: For constant mass, what does mΔv represent?
Answers: The change in momentum.

Questions: How is the force acting on an object related to its momentum?
Answers: force on an object = rate of change of momentum

Questions: What are examples of everyday safety features which increase the time for the change in momentum?
Answers: Airbags, seat belts, crumple zones and helmets.

Questions: What is elastic deformation?
Answers: object returns to original shape and size when forces are removed

Questions: What is inelastic deformation?
Answers: object does not return to original shape/size when forces are removed

Questions: How do you find the spring constant from a force–extension graph of a spring?
Answers: find the gradient of the straight‑line section

Questions: What is a transverse wave?
Answers: oscillations/vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer

Questions: What is a longitudinal wave?
Answers: oscillations/vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer

Questions: Give an example of a transverse wave.
Answers: electromagnetic waves

Questions: Give an example of a longitudinal wave.
Answers: sound waves

Questions: What is a compression?
Answers: Region of a longitudinal wave where particles are close together.

Questions: What is a rarefaction?
Answers: Region of a longitudinal wave where particles are further apart.

Questions: What is the amplitude of a wave?
Answers: maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position

Questions: What is the wavelength of a wave?
Answers: distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave

Questions: What is the frequency of a wave?
Answers: number of waves passing a fixed point per second

Questions: What unit is frequency measured in?
Answers: hertz (Hz)

Questions: What property of a wave always stays the same when it travels from one medium to another?
Answers: frequency

Questions: What rule do waves follow when they reflect off a surface?
Answers: angle of incidence = angle of reflection

Questions: What may happen to a wave transmitted into a different medium?
Answers: Its speed may change, causing refraction if it enters at an angle.

Questions: What happens when waves are absorbed by a substance?
Answers: energy of the wave is transferred to energy stores of the substance

Questions: Are electromagnetic (EM) waves longitudinal or transverse waves?
Answers: transverse

Questions: Explain why EM waves are not mechanical waves.
Answers: They can travel through a vacuum.

Questions: What do EM waves transfer from their source to an absorber?
Answers: energy

Questions: List the EM spectrum in order of decreasing wavelength.
Answers: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X‑rays, gamma

Questions: Which part of the EM spectrum can humans see?
Answers: visible light

Questions: How can electromagnetic waves be produced?
Answers: By accelerating electric charges; gamma rays can also come from nuclear changes.

Questions: How are gamma rays produced?
Answers: changes in the nucleus of an atom (e.g., radioactive decay)

Questions: How can radio waves be produced?
Answers: oscillations in an electrical circuit

Questions: How can we detect radio waves?
Answers: An aerial absorbs the waves and produces an alternating current of the same frequency.

Questions: What are radio waves used for?
Answers: transmitting television, mobile phone, and Bluetooth signals

Questions: What are microwaves used for?
Answers: satellite communications; cooking food

Questions: What is infrared radiation used for?
Answers: heating, remote controls, infrared cameras, cooking food

Questions: Which high-frequency EM waves can damage body cells?
Answers: Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

Questions: What are the hazards of being exposed to ultraviolet radiation?
Answers: Skin damage, including sunburn and increased skin-cancer risk; eye damage.

Questions: Why are X‑rays used for medical imaging?
Answers: Bone absorbs more X-rays than soft tissue, creating image contrast.

Questions: Why are gamma rays used for treating cancer and sterilising medical equipment?
Answers: High doses kill cancer cells and microorganisms.

Questions: What is the difference between a concave and convex lens?
Answers: convex bulges out in the middle; concave is thinner in the middle than at the edges

Questions: What does a convex lens do to parallel rays of light?
Answers: light converges at the principal focus

Questions: What does a concave lens do to parallel rays of light?
Answers: light diverges so rays appear to come from the principal focus

Questions: What is the focal length of a lens?
Answers: distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus

Questions: What kind of images do concave and convex lenses produce?
Answers: concave = virtual; convex = real or virtual

Questions: What determines the colour of monochromatic light?
Answers: Its frequency (or its wavelength in a vacuum).

Questions: What four things can happen to visible light when it hits an object?
Answers: transmitted, absorbed, reflected, refracted

Questions: What is the difference between specular and diffuse reflection?
Answers: specular from smooth surfaces; diffuse from rough surfaces

Questions: What words describe an object that transmits visible light?
Answers: transparent or translucent

Questions: Why does an object appear opaque?
Answers: does not transmit visible light – absorbs and reflects it

Questions: How do colour filters work?
Answers: absorb certain wavelengths; transmit others

Questions: What is refraction?
Answers: A change in wave direction caused by a change in speed at a boundary.

Questions: If a wave slows as it enters a medium at an angle, which way does it bend?
Answers: Towards the normal.

Questions: What is electric current?
Answers: rate of flow of charge

Questions: What units are charge, current, and time measured in?
Answers: coulombs (C), amperes (A), seconds (s) respectively

Questions: In a single-loop circuit, what is the same at every point?
Answers: The current.

Questions: What must there be in a closed circuit so that electrical charge can flow?
Answers: source of potential difference (p.d.)

Questions: Which two factors does current depend on and what are their units?
Answers: resistance in ohms (Ω); p.d. in volts (V)

Questions: What happens to the current if the resistance is increased but the p.d. stays the same?
Answers: current decreases

Questions: What is an ohmic conductor?
Answers: Current is proportional to p.d. at constant temperature, so resistance stays constant.

Questions: What happens to the resistance of a filament lamp as its temperature increases?
Answers: resistance increases

Questions: What happens to the resistance of a thermistor as its temperature increases?
Answers: resistance decreases

Questions: What happens to the resistance of an LDR when light intensity increases?
Answers: resistance decreases

Questions: What are the main features of a series circuit?
Answers: same current through each component; p.d. shared; total resistance is the sum

Questions: What are the main features of parallel resistors?
Answers: Equal p.d. across branches; branch currents add; total resistance is less than any branch resistance.

Questions: What is a non-renewable energy resource?
Answers: A resource used faster than it is replaced; it will eventually run out.

Questions: What is a renewable energy resource?
Answers: A resource that is replenished as it is used.

Questions: Name the main renewable and non-renewable energy resources.
Answers: Renewable: solar, tidal, wave, wind, geothermal, biofuel, hydroelectric. Non-renewable: coal, oil, gas, nuclear fuel.

Questions: What are the main advantages of using coal as an energy resource?
Answers: Reliable; electricity output can be adjusted to demand.

Questions: What are the main disadvantages of using coal as an energy resource?
Answers: Finite fuel; burning it releases CO₂ and air pollutants.

Questions: What are the main advantages of using nuclear fuel as an energy resource?
Answers: Much energy from little fuel; reliable output; very low CO₂ emissions during operation.

Questions: What are the main disadvantages of using nuclear fuel as an energy resource?
Answers: Radioactive waste needs safe storage; construction and decommissioning are costly.

Questions: What are the main advantages of using solar energy?
Answers: Renewable; no fuel cost or direct emissions while operating.

Questions: What are the main disadvantages of using solar energy?
Answers: No electricity at night; output falls in cloudy weather; installation can be costly.

Questions: What are the main advantages of using tidal power?
Answers: Predictable tides; no fuel cost or direct emissions while operating.

Questions: What are the main disadvantages of using tidal power?
Answers: High construction cost; may disrupt habitats and shipping; output varies with the tides.

Questions: What are the main advantages of using wave turbines?
Answers: Renewable; no fuel cost or direct emissions while operating.

Questions: What are the main disadvantages of using wave turbines?
Answers: Output depends on waves; installation is costly and may affect marine life or shipping.

Questions: What are the main disadvantages of using wind turbines?
Answers: Output depends on wind; turbines may cause noise or visual impacts.

Questions: What are the advantages and disadvantages of geothermal energy?
Answers: Advantages: reliable and low direct emissions. Disadvantages: costly to install and location-dependent.

Questions: What are the advantages and disadvantages of biofuels?
Answers: Advantages: fuel can be stored and replaced. Disadvantages: growing it uses land and may cause emissions.

Questions: What are the advantages and disadvantages of hydroelectric power?
Answers: Advantages: controllable output and no fuel cost. Disadvantages: dams are costly and can flood habitats.

Questions: Describe the basic structure of an atom.
Answers: nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons in fixed energy levels/shells

Questions: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
Answers: sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it

Questions: What charges do protons, neutrons, and electrons carry?
Answers: protons = positive, neutrons = no charge, electrons = negative

Questions: Why do atoms have no overall charge?
Answers: equal numbers of positive protons and negative electrons

Questions: What is the radius of an atom?
Answers: around 1×10⁻¹⁰ m

Questions: What is ionisation?
Answers: An atom gains or loses electrons and becomes an ion.

Questions: What is the mass number of an element?
Answers: number of protons + number of neutrons

Questions: Which particle do atoms of the same element always have the same number of?
Answers: protons

Questions: What are isotopes?
Answers: atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons

Questions: What were two main conclusions from the alpha particle scattering experiment?
Answers: Most of the atom is empty space; a tiny, positively charged nucleus contains most of its mass.

Questions: What are the three types of nuclear radiation?
Answers: alpha, beta, gamma

Questions: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most ionising?
Answers: alpha

Questions: How far do alpha, beta and gamma radiation travel through air?
Answers: Alpha: a few cm. Beta: around 1 m. Gamma: much further, with no fixed range.

Questions: What are the equation symbols for alpha and beta particles?
Answers: ⁴₂He (α) and ⁰₋₁e (β⁻).

Questions: What is meant by the half‑life of a radioactive source?
Answers: Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay, or for the source’s count rate above background to halve.

Questions: What is radioactive contamination?
Answers: unwanted presence of substances containing radioactive atoms on or in materials

Questions: Where does background radiation come from?
Answers: rocks, cosmic rays, fallout from weapons testing, nuclear accidents

Questions: Why are gamma‑emitting sources used for medical tracers and imaging?
Answers: gamma passes through body with relatively less damage to cells

Questions: What is nuclear fusion?
Answers: when two light nuclei join to make a heavier one

Questions: How can neutron-induced nuclear fission occur?
Answers: A heavy nucleus absorbs a neutron, splits into two smaller nuclei and releases energy and more neutrons.

Questions: What is a fluid?
Answers: a substance that can flow (liquid or gas)

Questions: What is the unit of pressure equal to one newton per square metre?
Answers: pascal (Pa)

Questions: Why does the pressure in a liquid increase with depth?
Answers: pressure at a point is due to weight of liquid above that point

Questions: Why does the pressure in a liquid depend on the liquid’s density?
Answers: weight of a liquid depends on its density

Questions: What is upthrust?
Answers: upward resultant force due to greater pressure on the bottom surface than the top

Questions: If weight and upthrust are the only forces on a fully submerged object and they are equal, what is its vertical acceleration?
Answers: Zero.

Questions: What will an object do if its weight is greater than the upthrust?
Answers: sink

Questions: Why does an object denser than a fluid sink in it?
Answers: Its weight exceeds the upthrust when fully submerged.

Questions: Why does an object less dense than a fluid float in it?
Answers: When fully submerged, upthrust exceeds its weight; it rises until the forces balance.

Questions: Does a partially submerged object experience greater pressure on its bottom or top surface?
Answers: bottom

Questions: What is the Earth’s atmosphere?
Answers: the layer of air that surrounds the Earth

Questions: What is atmospheric pressure caused by?
Answers: air molecules colliding with surfaces

Questions: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease with increased altitude?
Answers: less weight of air above; lower air density at higher altitude

Questions: How does the height of the atmosphere compare to the Earth’s radius?
Answers: it is much smaller

Questions: What is a magnetic field?
Answers: the region around a magnet where a magnetic material experiences a force

Questions: What happens when like and unlike poles are brought together?
Answers: like repel; unlike attract

Questions: What happens to the strength of a magnetic field with distance from the magnet?
Answers: decreases

Questions: Where is a magnet’s field strongest?
Answers: at the poles

Questions: Outside a magnet, which way do magnetic field lines point?
Answers: From north to south.

Questions: What does the spacing of magnetic field lines indicate?
Answers: closer lines = stronger field

Questions: What is a permanent magnet?
Answers: material that produces its own magnetic field

Questions: What is an induced magnet?
Answers: material that becomes magnetic when placed in a magnetic field

Questions: What does a magnetic compass contain?
Answers: small bar magnet

Questions: What is produced around a wire when an electric current flows?
Answers: a magnetic field

Questions: What factors affect field strength around a straight wire?
Answers: size of current; distance from wire

Questions: What effect does shaping a current‑carrying wire into a solenoid have?
Answers: increases magnetic field strength

Questions: How can the field inside a solenoid be increased?
Answers: put an iron core inside

Questions: What does Fleming’s left‑hand rule show?
Answers: relative orientation of force, current, and magnetic field for the motor effect

Questions: What is the symbol for magnetic flux density and its unit?
Answers: B; tesla (T)

Questions: What is the motor effect?
Answers: A current-carrying conductor experiences a force in a magnetic field.

Questions: What causes the motor effect?
Answers: interaction between the field from the current and the external magnetic field

Questions: What do loudspeakers and headphones do?
Answers: use the motor effect to convert current variations into sound waves

Questions: What does a material’s thermal conductivity tell you?
Answers: how well it conducts heat

Questions: Which materials have low thermal conductivity?
Answers: thermal insulators

Questions: Give three factors that determine the rate of thermal energy transfer through a material.
Answers: thermal conductivity; temperature difference; thickness

Questions: What factors affect the rate of heat loss from a building?
Answers: thickness and thermal conductivity of walls/roof; temperature difference

Questions: Define specific heat capacity.
Answers: Energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.

Questions: What are the main objects in our Solar System?
Answers: Sun, (eight) planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, comets

Questions: What kind of object is the Sun?
Answers: star

Questions: Which galaxy is the Solar System in?
Answers: the Milky Way

Questions: What do all stars start off as?
Answers: a huge cloud of gas and dust called a nebula

Questions: Which force forms a protostar from a nebula?
Answers: gravity

Questions: What outward effect does fusion have in a star?
Answers: Energy released by fusion produces outward pressure that opposes gravity.

Questions: How does a main sequence star remain stable?
Answers: outward forces from fusion balance gravitational forces

Questions: What determines a star’s life cycle?
Answers: mass

Questions: What is the life cycle of a Sun‑like star?
Answers: protostar → main sequence → red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf

Questions: What is the life cycle of a much more massive star?
Answers: protostar → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole (if mass high enough)

Questions: How do stars form elements up to iron?
Answers: By fusion of lighter nuclei.

Questions: Which elements are only produced in a supernova?
Answers: elements heavier than iron

Questions: How are elements distributed throughout the universe?
Answers: by massive stars going supernova

Questions: How does gravity change velocity but not speed in circular orbits?
Answers: gravity provides centripetal force; direction changes but speed may be constant

Questions: How can a satellite move into a stable orbit with a different speed?
Answers: Change to an orbit of a different radius.

Questions: What is red‑shift?
Answers: wavelengths appear longer if the source moves away from the observer

Questions: What evidence suggests the universe is expanding?
Answers: more distant galaxies show greater red‑shift (moving away faster)

Questions: What is the name of the theory for the origin of the universe?
Answers: the Big Bang theory

Questions: What is a scalar quantity?
Answers: only has a size (magnitude)

Questions: What is a vector quantity?
Answers: has both a size and direction

Questions: What is a force?
Answers: a push or pull that acts on an object due to interaction with another object

Questions: Is force a vector or scalar quantity?
Answers: vector

Questions: What is a contact force?
Answers: when objects are physically touching (e.g., friction, air‑resistance, tension, normal contact)

Questions: What is a non‑contact force?
Answers: when objects are physically separated (e.g., gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic)

Questions: What is the same about the interaction pair when two objects interact?
Answers: They have equal magnitude and act on different objects.

Questions: What is different about the interaction pair when two objects interact?
Answers: They act in opposite directions.

Questions: What is the resultant force if forces on an object are balanced?
Answers: zero

Questions: What is the centre of mass?
Answers: the point through which the weight of an object can be considered to act

Questions: What is the turning effect of a force called?
Answers: a moment

Questions: What about the moments on a balanced object?
Answers: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments

Questions: How does a lever reduce the force needed for a given moment?
Answers: by increasing the distance from the pivot

Questions: What happens to the moment when a small gear drives a large gear?
Answers: moment is increased

Questions: What does Newton’s First Law say?
Answers: an object’s velocity changes only if a resultant force acts

Questions: What is the resultant force on an object that remains at rest?
Answers: Zero.

Questions: What is the resultant force on an object moving at steady speed in a straight line?
Answers: zero

Questions: What does Newton’s Third Law say?
Answers: when two objects interact they exert equal and opposite forces on each other

Questions: How do you find the speed from a distance–time graph if the object is accelerating?
Answers: Find the gradient of a tangent at that point.

Questions: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
Answers: speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector (has direction)

Questions: What factors affect the speed a person walks, runs, or cycles?
Answers: age, fitness, terrain, distance travelled

Questions: What are typical speeds for walking, running, and cycling?
What are typical speeds of a car and a train?
Answers: 13–30 m/s and ~50 m/s respectively

Questions: What is a typical speed for sound in air?
What is acceleration?
Answers: change in velocity per second

Questions: What is the unit of acceleration?
Answers: m/s²

Questions: How can an object be accelerating at steady speed?
Answers: if its direction is changing

Questions: Does negative acceleration always mean an object is slowing down?
Answers: No. It slows down only when acceleration is opposite to its velocity.

Questions: What does the gradient of a distance–time graph give?
Answers: speed

Questions: What does the gradient of a velocity–time graph give?
Answers: acceleration

Questions: What does the area under a velocity–time graph give?
Answers: Displacement; for distance, add the magnitudes of the areas above and below the time axis.
